well that's a lovely sentence. I read the article and idk what it's talking about.

A current flows in a material when you apply a voltage to it. That current consists of charged particles, usually electrons. If you'd be dealing with a perfect material, you'd be accelerating these electrons constantly from one end of the material to the other. But they tend to get scattered (meaning they bump into stuff and get knocked back or veer off in a weird direction). That's what we measure as resistance. The main sources of scattering are, in order of importance: material impurities (dopants, vacancies, crystal defects, etc), phonons (heat vibrations) and other electrons.

If the electrons don't scatter each other much, so that you can ignore electron-electron interaction, you can consider the electrons to basically behave as a classical ideal gas. You can model the current with the so-called Drude model which says that electrons get accelerated until they get scattered, after which they accelerate again, until you get an average electron velocity (and thus current strength) in function of the applied voltage (which determines the strength of the acceleration). From there, you get I = V/R, Ohm's law.

Okay, now the Hall effect is what happens when you apply a magnetic field to a material through which a current flows. Moving charges are deflect by a magnetic field, so you end up steering the electrons to one side, perpendicular to the current direction. That then gives you a voltage across the material that you can measure, to determine things like the charge of the current carriers. Here's a picture.

The finaly piece is the viscosity. That means that in certain materials, like graphene, you can make the conditions so that electron-electron scattering is the dominant scattering mechanism. Which means the electrons will interact more with each other than with the material when it comes to carrying a current. This is fully analogous to getting turbulent flow in a gas. The electrons no longer neatly behave as ballistic particles being scattered by obstacles, but start forming swirls, eddies, backflow, etc. According to the article, this shows up in the Hall effect going wonky near the voltage contact. Apparently further out you end up in a laminar flow regime again, whereby the current behaves fairly normal. But anyway, due to the electrons behaving like a fluid, our simplified models no longer apply and we start having to take into account hydrodynamics.
